content: 1. The type of relationship each partner has with the World Health Organization (WHO) should be evaluated to identify potential areas for establishing new or stronger strategic partnerships. 2. WHO should actively participate in platforms and mechanisms for partner coordination, such as South-South and Triangular Cooperation, to enhance collaboration. 3. Regarding United Nations (UN) partners, it is essential to explore opportunities to leverage UN agency access and strategic collaboration with non-health ministries or sectors to promote a whole-of-government or health in all policies approach. 4. The UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and Common Country Analysis (CCA) should be utilized to inform the Country Cooperation Strategy (CCS) and vice versa. The CCS must reflect all UNSDCF outcomes and include additional outcomes as necessary. 5. If a country has expressed interest in the Global Action Plan for Healthy Lives and Well-being for All (GAP), which aims to strengthen collaboration among multilateral health organizations to accelerate progress on health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the presence and engagement of the 12 GAP agencies at the country level should be assessed. Priorities for closer collaboration on the seven accelerator themes and their linkages to the CCS should be discussed. 6. The 12 global agencies involved in the GAP include Gavi, the Global Financing Facility for Women, Children, and Adolescents, the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria, UNAIDS, UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, Unitaid, UN Women, the World Bank, the World Food Programme, and WHO. 7. The CCS should align with the GAP commitments, which include engaging with countries to identify health priorities, accelerating progress through joint action on programmatic themes, harmonizing operational and financial strategies, and reviewing progress to enhance shared accountability. 8. The CCS serves as a joint WHO-Member State instrument to implement the WHO’s General Programme of Work (GPW13) and its triple billion targets, ensuring alignment with the country’s health priorities and measurable outcomes. 9. The CCS informs and reinforces the health dimension of the UNSDCF, harmonizing WHO’s activities with those of other UN agencies and development partners to achieve the SDGs. 10. The UNSDCF, as the primary instrument for UN development activities in a country, provides programmatic guidance for UN agency programs and ensures greater political visibility for health issues, increasing the likelihood of donor funding. 11. WHO Country Offices (WCOs) should align the CCS with the UNSDCF to ensure health issues are prioritized in government agendas, policy coherence among UN agencies is maintained, and additional resources are leveraged. 12. WHO Representatives and UN Resident Coordinators are responsible for elevating the priority of health issues within the UNSDCF. 13. The CCS development process provides an opportunity to refine and improve previously agreed priorities to ensure they are strategically aligned with GPW13 and the national health agenda. 14. Strategic priorities in the CCS should be adapted to the SMART format (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, and time-bound) and should align with GPW13 outcomes while addressing the national health agenda. 15. The CCS should clearly define the roles and responsibilities of WHO at all levels in supporting government efforts and collaborating with partners. 16. Indicators and targets to measure the impact and results of each priority should be agreed upon during the CCS dialogue phase, ensuring alignment with national health indicators, GPW13 metrics, and SDG-related indicators. 17. The CCS should focus on the triple billion targets of GPW13: universal health coverage (UHC), health emergencies, and healthier populations, with program targets mapped out for implementation. 18. The CCS dialogue phase involves high-level strategic discussions, particularly at the ministerial level, as well as technical meetings and workshops to refine priorities and ensure alignment with national and global health goals. 19. Key stakeholders in the CCS process include government representatives, UN agencies, development partners, NGOs, civil society organizations, and, where necessary, health experts familiar with the country’s context. 20. The CCS should incorporate lessons learned from previous WHO and partner cooperation projects, ensuring that health priorities are realistic and adequately supported by WHO’s human and financial resources. 21. The CCS should address cross-cutting issues such as human rights, equity, and gender, ensuring these are high on the national agenda. 22. The CCS should align with the UNSDCF to ensure health issues receive top priority, policy coherence is maintained, and additional resources are leveraged from UN agencies and partners. 23. The CCS should include a robust impact framework aligned with GPW13 and national health plans, focusing on measurable outcomes for UHC, health emergencies, and healthier populations. 24. The CCS should ensure that health priorities are ambitious, realistic, and relevant to the country’s situation, with mechanisms for joint monitoring and evaluation of ongoing impact. 25. The CCS should emphasize WHO’s comparative advantage in policy dialogue, strategic support, technical assistance, and service delivery to address priority areas effectively.
